title: Strategies and Dependency Injection with Functions

contentBlocks.body: The strategy pattern replaces a growing if/else or switch with a lookup table of interchangeable functions that share one signature. Adding a new behaviour means adding an entry, not editing a branchy function that already works. In JavaScript you need no classes or interfaces for this: an object of functions is the strategy table.

Dependency injection is the same idea applied to collaborators. Instead of a function reaching out to a global (the clock, the database, fetch, Math.random), it receives what it needs as parameters. A factory function takes the dependencies once and returns the configured function. Tests then pass fakes, and production passes the real thing.
A useful smell test: if a function is hard to test because it calls Date.now(), fetch, or a module-level singleton, inject that dependency as a parameter with a sensible default.
Look up strategies with a guard. shippingStrategies["toString"] finds Object.prototype.toString, so user-supplied keys should be checked with Object.hasOwn(table, key) or the table built with a Map.

knowledgeItems.prompt: What is the main benefit of a strategy table over a long if/else chain?

choices: new behaviours are added as entries without editing working code
it removes the need for tests
payload.answer: new behaviours are added as entries without editing working code
payload.explanation: Each strategy is small and separate; the dispatcher never changes when a new one is added.

knowledgeItems.prompt: Why does createCheckout take now as a parameter instead of calling new Date() inside?

choices: because new Date() is not allowed in closures
so tests can pass a fixed clock and get deterministic output
because Date is only available in browsers
payload.answer: so tests can pass a fixed clock and get deterministic output
payload.explanation: Injecting the clock is dependency injection: the caller decides which implementation to use.

knowledgeItems.prompt: const s = { a: () => 1 }; what is typeof s["toString"]?

payload.explanation: Plain objects inherit toString from Object.prototype, so an unguarded lookup can find it. Guard with Object.hasOwn.
